title: Can small business owners access the credit they need?
gist: Using Small Business Credit Survey data in FRED covering 2016-2025, the share of applicant firms approved for the FULL amount of financing they sought is persistently highest for low-credit-risk firms and lowest for high-risk firms, which tend to be newer and smaller. The same dataset shows rural firms and firms with revenue above $1 million fare better than urban and sub-$1 million peers, while veteran-owned firms track non-veteran-owned firms closely. (The raw record carries no published date; the URL implies August 2026.)

themes.theme: Credit-risk tiering of small business financing

insights.claim: Small Business Credit Survey data charted in FRED show that, across every year from 2016 through 2025, the share of applicant firms approved for the full amount of financing sought was consistently higher for low-credit-risk firms than for medium- and high-credit-risk firms.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: The low/medium/high credit-risk approval series in FRED is a clean, decade-long spread indicator for small-business credit tightness; a widening low-vs-high gap flags stress at the marginal borrower before aggregate lending data move.
insights.quote: Survey responses are available from 2016 through 2025.

insights.claim: Federal Reserve small business researchers argue that firms with weaker credit scores are more often newer and smaller, so the businesses most in need of financing may be the ones with the most difficulty obtaining it.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Credit access is procyclical and concentrated against young, small firms, implying small-business formation and hiring are more rate- and credit-sensitive than headline data suggest; watch this cohort for early-cycle damage.
insights.quote: riskier firms are more often newer and smaller than those with stronger credit scores. As a result, it may be the case that businesses most in need of financing have the most difficulty accessing those funds.

themes.theme: Access gaps by geography, size and owner type

insights.claim: Small rural firms were consistently more likely than their urban counterparts to receive the full amount of financing they applied for, according to Small Business Credit Survey data.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Counters the common assumption that rural credit deserts dominate; community and regional bank relationships in rural markets appear to translate into better full-approval rates, a factor for regional bank small-business loan books.
insights.quote: Small rural firms were consistently more likely to receive the full amount of financing compared with their urban counterparts.

insights.claim: Among surveyed small businesses, those with annual revenues above $1 million were more likely to be approved for the full financing amount sought than firms with revenue below that threshold.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: The $1 million revenue line is an observable cutoff for credit access, marking where non-bank and fintech lenders have the largest addressable gap to fill.
insights.quote: Small firms with annual revenues above $1 million were more likely to receive the full amount of financing compared with firms with revenue below that threshold.

insights.claim: Veteran-owned small firms are generally on par with non-veteran-owned small firms in obtaining the full financing they request, with only occasional short-lived gaps between the two groups.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Suggests owner-demographic cuts are not uniformly informative; credit risk, firm size and revenue carry the real explanatory power, so screen on those rather than demographic categories.
insights.quote: But short-lived gaps between these two groups occasionally appear.

insights.claim: The national Small Business Credit Survey, produced with research from the 12 Reserve Banks of the Federal Reserve System, asks firms with fewer than 500 employees how much financing they sought and obtained over the past year, and its 'Approved for New Financing' release table is available in FRED broken out by credit risk, industry, firm size, geography and owner demographics.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A free, granular, survey-based read on small-business credit supply that can be tracked directly in FRED - useful for cross-checking bank loan-officer surveys and regional bank credit commentary.
insights.quote: The SBCS asks firms with fewer than 500 employees how much financing their business sought and obtained in the past year.
